contribution: Jegede and Aikenhead examined how pupils move between their everyday culture and ==the culture of school science==.
They reviewed ==collateral learning theory==, explaining how pupils cope with conflicting worldviews.
They proposed the teacher as a ==‘culture broker’==, supported by culturally sensitive curriculum and assessment.
today: More than 25 years on, debates about ==Indigenous knowledge==, culturally responsive teaching and equity give it renewed relevance.
The paper still challenges assumptions about ==whose knowledge== school science privileges.
Can science be made accessible without asking students to ==abandon their cultural identities==?

🌍 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝𝐬? In this 1999 article, Olugbemiro J. Jegede and Glen S. Aikenhead explored how students negotiate the borders between their everyday culture and the culture of school science. They proposed the science teacher as a ‘𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗿’, an idea that speaks directly to today’s debates on 𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 and equity. https://doi.org/10.1080/0263514990170104
